```{r library}
library(koine)
```

## Why

An analyst has just fitted a mixed model -- a random intercept for the
blocks in a trial, or two crossed intercepts for variety and trial in a
multi-environment trial (MET) -- and wants an independent second opinion:
not another run of the same sampler on the same posterior, but an opinion
built from inference methods and model-structure variants that are
genuinely different from whatever produced the first fit. Does a
heavy-tailed alternative agree with a Gaussian fit? Does a closed-form
treatment of the random effects agree with what a sampler-based fit
reported? koine answers by stacking over a curated battery of inference
lenses in predictive space and returning one synthesised opinion, or by
abstaining outright -- declining to guess -- when the battery cannot offer
enough independent perspectives to say anything. This vignette walks the
full spine an analyst
would use to get that opinion: the request, the battery that resolves
against it, a single lens, the diversity that makes a synthesis worth
having, and the two mixed-model shapes koine supports -- a single random
intercept and a multi-environment trial's two crossed intercepts -- ending
with what koine does when it should not answer at all.

## What

A `koine_pass()` is an engine-neutral, declarative request: it carries the
formula, the data, an evaluable family, the canonical observation axis, and
a content hash, and it is the one object every lens and every synthesis
call reads. `resolve_battery()` enrols only the lenses whose family,
feature support and tier fit that request, and records why every other
lens was excluded, so absence is always explained rather than silent. A
lens's own `fit_*()` function -- `fit_dram()`, `fit_robust_t()`,
`fit_glmm_marginal()`, and others in the registry -- takes a pass and
returns draws, or a typed abstention if the lens cannot field the model.
`synthesise()` is the front door: it resolves the battery, fits every
opinion lens, gates on PSIS reliability, and stacks the survivors into one
predictive opinion, reporting the stacking weights, the effective number of
distinct components, and an over-dispersed envelope that reflects
between-lens disagreement as well as within-lens uncertainty. `abstention()`
and `is_abstention()` make a decline a typed, first-class value rather than
an error or a silently wrong number.

## Do

### The request: a pass

```{r toy-population}
set.seed(42)
n_pop <- 40L
x_pop <- rnorm(n_pop)
d_pop <- data.frame(
  y = 1.5 + 0.8 * x_pop + rnorm(n_pop, sd = 0.7), x = x_pop
)
pass <- koine_pass(y ~ x, data = d_pop, family = gaussian())
pass
```

The family is wrapped into an *evaluable* `family_spec`: koine computes the
pointwise log-likelihood itself, because the upstream family object exposes
a mean function but no log-likelihood.

```{r family}
fs <- as_family_spec(gaussian())
fs$loglik_pointwise(y = c(0, 1), eta = c(0, 1), aux = list(sigma = 1))
```

### The battery

```{r resolve}
resolved <- resolve_battery(pass)
vapply(resolved$enrolled, function(lens) lens$id, character(1))
```

```{r resolve-excluded-kable, echo = FALSE}
excluded_df <- data.frame(
  lens = vapply(resolved$excluded, `[[`, character(1), "id"),
  reason = vapply(resolved$excluded, `[[`, character(1), "reason"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(
  excluded_df, col.names = c("Lens", "Reason excluded"),
  caption = "Lenses excluded from this Gaussian population battery."
)
```

Seven lenses resolve for this Gaussian population model: DRAM, NIMBLE-Gibbs
and DREAM (different inference families on the same posterior), plus the
model-structure variants -- robust-t and a shrinkage spectrum (ridge, lasso,
horseshoe). The table shows why every other registered lens was left out;
the Polya-Gamma Gibbs lens, for instance, is excluded on family grounds
because it serves binomial logistic models, not Gaussian ones, while the
random-effects lenses are excluded because this particular pass has no
grouping term for them to honour.

### One lens: delayed-rejection adaptive Metropolis

```{r dram}
fit_pop <- fit_dram(pass, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L, n_chains = 2L)
fit_pop
```

```{r dram-kable, echo = FALSE}
sm_pop <- as.data.frame(posterior::summarise_draws(fit_pop$draws, "mean", "sd"))
knitr::kable(
  sm_pop, digits = 3,
  caption = "DRAM posterior summary for the population regression."
)
```

### Diversity: a heavy-tailed structure variant

koine's value as a second opinion comes from *diversity*. Lenses that fit
the same model structure only corroborate one another -- a useful
consistency check, but the stacking weights then collapse onto a single
component. Genuine diversity needs a different model *structure*. The
robust-t lens supplies one: a Student-t likelihood whose heavy tails give a
materially different predictive when the data depart from Gaussianity. The
battery below is restricted to two lenses -- DRAM and robust-t -- on a
synthetic, moderately heavy-tailed toy, so the comparison is exactly this
one contrast rather than the full seven-lens battery above.

### Engines available on this build

Two later sections need an optional package each: the two figures below
need `ggplot2`, and the MET corroboration check needs `lme4`. Each guarded
chunk checks for its own package and prints one sentence in its place when
the package is absent, so the vignette still renders, with less to read, on
a build that carries neither.

```{r engines}
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_lme4 <- requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r toy-heavy}
set.seed(19)
n_ht <- 60L
x_ht <- rnorm(n_ht)
y_ht <- 1 + 0.8 * x_ht + rt(n_ht, df = 5) * 0.6      # moderately heavy-tailed
pass_ht <- koine_pass(y_ht ~ x_ht, data.frame(y_ht = y_ht, x_ht = x_ht),
                      gaussian())

reg <- koine_stage1_registry()
lens_id <- function(id) which(vapply(reg, function(z) z$id, "") == id)
reg_ht <- list(reg[[lens_id("dram")]], reg[[lens_id("robust_t")]])
reg_ht[[1]]$fit_fn <- function(p, ls) fit_dram(p, ls, 1500L, 750L, 2L)
reg_ht[[2]]$fit_fn <- function(p, ls) {
  fit_robust_t(p, ls, nu = 4, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L, n_chains = 2L)
}
res_ht <- synthesise(pass_ht, registry = reg_ht)
res_ht
```

```{r toy-heavy-independence-kable, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(
  res_ht$independence[, c("lens_id", "family", "kernel")],
  col.names = c("Lens", "Sampler family", "Kernel"),
  caption = "Independence declaration for the two-lens heavy-tailed battery."
)
```

```{r toy-heavy-facts, echo = FALSE}
w_ht <- res_ht$opinion$weights
n_eff_ht <- res_ht$diagnostics$weight_concentration$n_eff
lpe_ht <- res_ht$diagnostics$linear_pool_envelope
n_outside_ht <- sum(lpe_ht$flags$n_outside > 0L)
```

### Figure: the stacking weights

```{r fig-weights, eval = has_ggplot2, echo = has_ggplot2, fig.cap = "Stacking weights for the two-lens heavy-tailed battery, with the effective-component count n_eff annotated. Neither lens is at zero, so the mixture is a genuine blend, not a corroboration collapse onto one structure.", fig.alt = "Horizontal bar chart of stacking weights for the dram and robust_t lenses, both between roughly 0.4 and 0.6, with the effective-component count n_eff printed in the title."}
weight_df <- data.frame(
  lens = names(w_ht), weight = as.numeric(w_ht), stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ggplot2::ggplot(
  weight_df, ggplot2::aes(x = stats::reorder(lens, weight), y = weight,
                          fill = lens)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col() +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "lens", y = "stacking weight",
    title = sprintf("n_eff = %.2f effective lens(es)", n_eff_ht)
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig-weights-skip, eval = !has_ggplot2, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("ggplot2 is not installed; the stacking-weight figure is skipped.\n")
```

### Figure: the pooled predictive envelope

```{r fig-envelope, eval = has_ggplot2, echo = has_ggplot2, fig.cap = "The over-dispersed linear-pool envelope for the heavy-tailed battery: the pooled posterior-mean response (line) and its 95% envelope (band), built from the two lenses' means and their between-lens disagreement, against the fitted x range.", fig.alt = "Scatter of the heavy-tailed data with a shaded 95 percent envelope band around a pooled mean-response line, wide enough to contain nearly all points."}
ord_ht <- order(x_ht)
points_df <- data.frame(x = x_ht[ord_ht], y = y_ht[ord_ht])
band_df <- data.frame(
  x = x_ht[ord_ht], lower = lpe_ht$lower[ord_ht], upper = lpe_ht$upper[ord_ht],
  pool_mean = lpe_ht$pool_mean[ord_ht]
)
ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
    data = band_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
    fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = band_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = pool_mean), colour = "#0072B2",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = points_df, ggplot2::aes(x = x, y = y), colour = "grey35", size = 1.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "x", y = "y",
    title = "Pool envelope: pooled mean response and its 95% band"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r fig-envelope-skip, eval = !has_ggplot2, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("ggplot2 is not installed; the pool-envelope figure is skipped.\n")
```

### Mixed models: a random intercept

koine also handles a single random intercept, `(1 | g)`. The opinion is
built on an axis orthogonal to the sealed engines: NIMBLE-Gibbs
(`fit_nimble_glmm()`) *samples* the random effects, while the marginal lens
(`fit_glmm_marginal()`, shown here because it needs no extra toolchain)
*integrates* them out -- exactly for the Gaussian LMM, by adaptive
Gauss-Hermite quadrature for the binomial GLMM. Both report `(beta, sigma,
tau)` and are stacked on the same per-observation *integrated* predictive
(the random effect marginalised under each draw's variance components),
which keeps the leave-one-out gate reliable. (Poisson is enrolled alongside
Gaussian and binomial, on a funnel-safe blocked-slice kernel; a post-fit
convergence gate makes the lens abstain rather than contribute where the
variance component is too weakly identified to mix.)

```{r toy-re}
set.seed(20)
n_re <- 60L
n_groups_re <- 10L
g_re <- factor(rep(seq_len(n_groups_re), each = n_re / n_groups_re))
x_re <- rnorm(n_re)
b_re <- rnorm(n_groups_re, 0, 1.1)                  # group random intercepts
y_re <- 1 + 0.5 * x_re + b_re[g_re] + rnorm(n_re, 0, 0.7)
pass_re <- koine_pass(
  y_re ~ x_re + (1 | g_re), data.frame(y_re = y_re, x_re = x_re, g_re = g_re),
  gaussian()
)
fit_re <- fit_glmm_marginal(pass_re, n_iter = 1500L, n_burn = 750L,
                            n_chains = 2L)
```

```{r toy-re-kable, echo = FALSE}
sm_re <- as.data.frame(posterior::summarise_draws(fit_re$draws, "mean"))
knitr::kable(
  sm_re, digits = 3,
  caption = "Random-intercept marginal-lens posterior means (b0, sigma, tau)."
)
```

A third lens, `fit_glmm_robust_re()`, gives the random intercepts heavy
(Student-t) tails. Where the two Gaussian-RE lenses corroborate (their
weights collapse), this structure variant earns real stacking weight when
group effects are outlying -- so koine's mixed-model opinion, like its
population battery, becomes sensitive to model structure rather than a
weighted echo of one assumption.

### Multi-environment trials: variety and trial together

The breeder-standard multi-environment-trial (MET) model carries *two*
random intercepts -- a variety effect and a trial (environment) effect,
crossed (each variety grown across many trials) or nested. koine fits this
structure directly with `(1 | variety) + (1 | trial)`, so it corroborates a
production MET model on the model that model actually fits, not on a
single-random-effect reduction that discards the trial structure. The
Gaussian MET marginal stays exact: the random effects are integrated out
analytically, through a dense Cholesky of the marginal covariance

$$V = \sigma^2 I + \tau_{\text{variety}}^2 Z_{\text{variety}} Z_{\text{variety}}^\top +
\tau_{\text{trial}}^2 Z_{\text{trial}} Z_{\text{trial}}^\top,$$

where $Z_{\text{variety}}$ and $Z_{\text{trial}}$ are the (0/1) grouping
indicator matrices for each random factor and $\tau_{\text{variety}}$,
$\tau_{\text{trial}}$ are their variance-component standard deviations --
where the sealed engines instead sample (NIMBLE) or Laplace-approximate
(INLA) them. This is the one fitted example in this vignette that needs two
grouping factors rather than one: demonstrating that koine fits a crossed
structure at all is the entire point of the section, so the two groupings
stay, with every other dimension of the design shrunk instead.

```{r toy-met}
set.seed(404)
n_variety <- 10L                                    # varieties
n_trial <- 5L                                       # trials (environments)
u_variety <- rnorm(n_variety, 0, 1.0)                # variety effects
v_trial <- rnorm(n_trial, 0, 2.5)                    # trial effects (dominant)
rows_met <- vector("list", n_variety)
for (i in seq_len(n_variety)) {
  trials_i <- sample(seq_len(n_trial), 3L)          # incomplete, unbalanced
  obs_i <- lapply(trials_i, function(t) {
    data.frame(
      variety = i, trial = t,
      yield = 5 + u_variety[i] + v_trial[t] + rnorm(1L, 0, 0.6)
    )
  })
  rows_met[[i]] <- do.call(rbind, obs_i)
} # ends i, over the varieties
met <- do.call(rbind, rows_met)
met$variety <- factor(met$variety)
met$trial <- factor(met$trial)
nrow(met)

pass_met <- koine_pass(
  yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), met, gaussian(), seed = 5L
)
pass_met                                            # tagged [MET], crossed
fit_met <- fit_glmm_marginal(pass_met, n_iter = 1200L, n_burn = 600L,
                             n_chains = 2L)
```

```{r toy-met-kable, echo = FALSE}
sm_met <- as.data.frame(posterior::summarise_draws(fit_met$draws, "mean"))
knitr::kable(
  sm_met, digits = 3,
  caption = paste0(
    "MET marginal-lens posterior means (b0, sigma, tau_variety, tau_trial)."
  )
)
```

The draws carry one `tau_<grouping>` per random factor. The chunk below
checks koine's MET variety effects against a production MET model (here
`lme4`, fitted by REML), and against a single-random-intercept reduction
that confounds each variety with the trials it happened to be grown in.

```{r met-corroborate, eval = has_lme4, echo = has_lme4}
prod_fit <- lme4::lmer(
  yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), met, REML = TRUE
)
blup_prod <- lme4::ranef(prod_fit)$variety[, 1]
single_fit <- lme4::lmer(yield ~ 1 + (1 | variety), met, REML = TRUE)
blup_single <- lme4::ranef(single_fit)$variety[, 1]

# koine MET variety effects (GLS BLUP at the posterior-mean variance components)
mv_met <- stats::setNames(sm_met$mean, sm_met$variable)
design_met <- koine:::.pass_design(pass_met)
red_met <- koine:::.pass_re_design(pass_met)
taus_met <- c(mv_met["tau_variety"], mv_met["tau_trial"])
vmat_met <- koine:::.re_marginal_cov(
  design_met$N, red_met$factors, taus_met, mv_met["sigma"]
)
b_names <- paste0("b_", colnames(design_met$X))
resid_met <- design_met$y - as.numeric(design_met$X %*% mv_met[b_names])
z_variety <- koine:::.re_indicator(
  red_met$factors[[1L]]$group, red_met$factors[[1L]]$n_groups
)
u_koine <- as.numeric(
  taus_met[1L]^2 * t(z_variety) %*% solve(vmat_met, resid_met)
)

cor_met <- cor(u_koine, blup_prod)
cor_single <- cor(blup_single, blup_prod)
```

```{r met-corroborate-kable, eval = has_lme4, echo = FALSE}
cor_df <- data.frame(
  comparison = c("koine MET vs production MET", "single-RE vs production MET"),
  correlation = c(cor_met, cor_single)
)
knitr::kable(
  cor_df, digits = 4,
  caption = "Variety-effect correlation against the production (lme4) MET fit."
)
```

```{r met-corroborate-skip, eval = !has_lme4, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("lme4 is not installed; the MET corroboration check is skipped.\n")
```

A non-Gaussian MET -- whose dense crossed marginal has no exact quadrature
-- is declined outright rather than approximated:

```{r met-glmm-abstain}
counts_met <- transform(met, n = rpois(nrow(met), 4))
fit_glmm_marginal(
  koine_pass(n ~ 1 + (1 | variety) + (1 | trial), counts_met, poisson())
)$reason
```

Richer structure is refused rather than fitted as the wrong model: a random
slope, or more than two grouping factors, makes koine abstain
`feature_unsupported`.

```{r re-abstain}
pass_bad <- koine_pass(
  y_re ~ x_re + (x_re | g_re),
  data.frame(y_re = y_re, x_re = x_re, g_re = g_re), gaussian()
)
synthesise(pass_bad)$reason
```

### When koine abstains

Abstention is a first-class outcome, not an error. If fewer than two
independent opinion lenses resolve -- for instance with a single-lens
battery -- koine declines to guess and says why.

```{r abstain}
out_abstain <- synthesise(pass, registry = list(koine_stage1_registry()[[1]]))
is_abstention(out_abstain)
out_abstain
```

## Read

The DRAM lens recovers the data-generating intercept and slope closely:
`r round(sm_pop$mean[sm_pop$variable == "b_(Intercept)"], 2)` against a
true `1.5`, and `r round(sm_pop$mean[sm_pop$variable == "b_x"], 2)` against
a true `0.8`.

On the heavy-tailed toy, the two-lens battery does not collapse onto a
single structure: DRAM carries
`r round(w_ht[["dram"]], 2)` of the stacking weight and robust-t carries
`r round(w_ht[["robust_t"]], 2)`, giving `r round(n_eff_ht, 2)` effective
lens(es) -- above the package's degeneracy threshold of 1.5, so the
diagnostic records genuine diversity rather than a corroboration collapse.
The weights figure shows that split directly, and the envelope figure shows
what it buys: a pooled band wide enough that, on this particular draw,
`r n_outside_ht` of the `r n_ht` points fall outside the 95% band even
though the band is inflated for between-lens disagreement as well as
within-lens uncertainty.

```{r read-re, echo = FALSE}
re_intercept <- round(sm_re$mean[sm_re$variable == "b_(Intercept)"], 2)
re_slope <- round(sm_re$mean[sm_re$variable == "b_x_re"], 2)
re_sigma <- round(sm_re$mean[sm_re$variable == "sigma"], 2)
re_tau <- round(sm_re$mean[sm_re$variable == "tau"], 2)
```

The single-random-intercept marginal lens recovers the data-generating
values in the same qualitative way: intercept `r re_intercept` (true `1`),
slope `r re_slope` (true `0.5`), residual SD `r re_sigma` (true `0.7`) and
group SD `r re_tau` (true `1.1`), on `r n_re` observations in
`r n_groups_re` groups -- fewer groups than a production analysis would
carry, which is why the variance component is recovered only qualitatively
rather than to two decimal places.

```{r read-met, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
if (has_lme4) {
  cat(
    "On the multi-environment toy, koine's MET marginal variety effects",
    "correlate", sprintf("%.4f", cor_met),
    "with the production (`lme4`) MET fit, against",
    sprintf("%.4f", cor_single),
    "for the single-random-intercept reduction that ignores the trial",
    "structure. The gap between the two reproduces, at this much smaller",
    "scale, the qualitative point the section makes: confounding a",
    "variety with the trials it happened to be grown in costs real",
    "agreement with the model that actually generated the data, even on",
    "an incomplete, unbalanced design of only", nrow(met), "records.\n"
  )
} else {
  cat(
    "lme4 is not installed on this build, so the correlation between",
    "koine's MET marginal fit and a production MET model is not computed",
    "here; the section above states which check was skipped.\n"
  )
}
```

Every abstention in this vignette is grounded in the same registry the
battery table used above: the Poisson MET call, the random-slope call, and
the single-lens `synthesise()` call all decline through the typed
`koine_abstention` path (`is_abstention()` returns `TRUE` for the last of
the three) rather than returning a silently wrong number.

## Limits

The random-effects lenses carry a fixed weakly-informative prior --
`N(0, 5)` on every fixed-effect coefficient and `lognormal(0, 2)` on every
variance-component standard deviation for the Gaussian and binomial
families -- and `koine_pass()`'s `prior` argument, though present in the
signature, does not reach them: it is reserved for lenses that do not yet
exist. On a response measured in the tens or hundreds this reference prior
pulls the intercept toward zero and lets the group standard deviation
absorb the resulting offset, because the prior's own scale, not the data's,
starts to dominate the posterior. The examples in this vignette are
engineered on roughly unit scale for exactly this reason: they are not a
demonstration that the prior is harmless, only that it is invisible when
the design already matches its assumption. A caller with a response in
its raw, natural units -- yield in kilograms per hectare, a count in the
hundreds, anything not already standardised -- should centre and scale the
response and every non-intercept covariate before building the pass, and
map any recovered coefficients back to the original scale afterwards; the
random-intercept and MET marginal lenses in this vignette would return a
materially different, prior-dominated opinion on the same data left in its
natural units.

Every fitted example in this vignette uses at most 60 observations and a
few hundred to two thousand MCMC iterations over two chains, chosen so the
whole vignette renders in under two minutes rather than to reflect the
scale koine is meant to run at; the MET section is the one exception,
because demonstrating a crossed two-grouping structure at all needs two
grouping factors, so it shrinks every other dimension of the design
instead. The two-lens diversity split shown above is itself sensitive to
this small a sample: at `n = 60`, most seeds tried while preparing this
vignette gave a degenerate, single-lens-dominated split rather than the
genuine two-lens blend shown here, whereas the same scenario at a few
hundred observations is far less seed-sensitive. A reader who wants a
diversity diagnostic that does not depend on which random draw they
happened to get should run the same battery at production scale, not at
this vignette's render-time scale.

The MET marginal is exact only for the Gaussian identity-link case; a
non-Gaussian MET routes through a marginalised sampler that can itself
abstain on convergence grounds, and that sampler is not exercised in this
vignette (the Poisson MET example above abstains before any sampling is
attempted, because the structure itself, not a convergence failure, is
what is declined). koine's random-effects corner is limited throughout to
a single random intercept or the two-grouping MET structure: random
slopes, correlated random effects, and more than two crossed or nested
groupings are all refused rather than approximated, as the random-slope
example above shows.

## What to read next

The package's own `INTEGRATION.md` (installed alongside the package,
`system.file("INTEGRATION.md", package = "koine")`) specifies the contract
a parent triangulation package drives to use koine as a fourth, synthesised
witness, including the exact supported-model corner this vignette
exercises. The **quorum** package's *Getting started with quorum* vignette
shows koine consumed as one lens in a wider quorum of independent
estimates, through its `emit_koine()` wrapper; that wrapper standardises
the response and covariates before calling koine, which is the practical
answer to the prior-scale limit stated above.

## Reproduce

Seeds are set per section (`42` for the population regression, `19` for
the heavy-tailed diversity toy, `20` for the random-intercept toy, `404`
for the MET toy) so each fitted example is reproducible on its own; package
versions follow.

```{r session-info}
sessionInfo()
```
